newsitem.title: USA: Two oil refiners to help build heating oil supply.
newsitem.headline: Two oil refiners to help build heating oil supply.

text.p: At least two refiners pledged to take steps to beef up heating oil supplies ahead of this winter to help ease fears of a potential shortage, Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary said Friday.
But the government itself had no plans to buy heating oil to shore up stocks, which are at extremely low levels, she said, following a meeting with executives from 16 oil and gas companies.
But even if there are no shortages, consumers are likely to face higher prices this winter than last.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration is still predicting average heating oil prices this winter will be 9 cents a gallon higher than last winter, although the current retail price of $1.11 is 20 cents higher than a year ago.

At a news conference, O'Leary said, "On the question of distillate we've reached the conclusion for the near term that the market certainly does not need Big Brother as a big buyer." Distillates are oil products including heating oil.
"The question is if those inventories remain as low as they have over the past four to five weeks and the pace of production of distillates continues, most believe that will meet the need," she said.
U.S. refiner Citgo, which is owned by Petroleos de Venezuela, offered to delay planned maintenance on a unit at one of its refineries, she said.
Tosco Corp. said it would boost output from its New Jersey refinery earlier than planned.

Heating oil stocks on the East Coast, which consumes 75 percent of all heating oil in the United States, stood at 18 million barrels or 43 percent lower than a year ago at the end of last week, according to the Energy Department's tally.
Tosco said it would focus its heating oil sales in the Northeast.

Asked if she had urged oil companies to hold back exports of heating oil which have been flowing to Europe, as suggested by Representative Joe Kennedy, D.-Mass., O'Leary said, "I have not asked, and no one who works with me has asked nor indicated to the private sector ... to halt distillates from the U.S."
"And in any case, we have no authority to do so," she added.
Kennedy was among the first lawmakers to raise alarm about the heating oil situation last month.
While O'Leary promised to study a proposal by Kennedy to set up a regional oil product reserve to help cope with emergencies, Kennedy said the government was not doing enough to prevent a crisis now.

"Today's meeting is an important first step to solving this problem. However, it will not result in inventory levels that are sufficiently high to protect American consumers from potentially devastating price hikes," Kennedy said in a statement.
Several executives suggested oil futures trading was partly to blame for the lack of physical stockbuilding.
"Some in this meeting that we held raised deep conern about trading in petroleum product futures," she said.

Analysts and traders have said that the unusual configuration of futures prices, with current heating oil prices higher than prices in future months, discouraged refiners from building stocks because they were expecting prices to fall.

Of the 20 companies invited to Friday's meeting, 16 sent representatives, including majors Amerada Hess Corp., represented by chairman Leon Hess, Exxon Corp., Mobil Corp., Texaco Inc. and Shell Oil, the U.S. subsidiary of Royal Dutch/Shell.
